Common innervation of the renal pelvis and testicle via T11–T12
questions.correctAnswer: E) Common innervation of the renal pelvis and testicle via T11–T12
questions.correctAnswerText: Common innervation of the renal pelvis and testicle via T11–T12
questions.explanation: The renal pelvis and testicle share afferent innervation at the T11–T12 spinal levels, explaining why renal pain can be referred to the testis and vice versa. This differs from radiating pain, which spreads along a single dermatome.

questions.text: A patient presents with colicky flank pain, no fever, and is observed constantly moving and rolling in bed unable to find a comfortable position. What is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.correctAnswer: A) Ureteric obstruction from a stone
questions.explanation: Colicky, fluctuating pain with the "rolling sign" (patient unable to lie still) and absence of fever is characteristic of obstructive stone disease rather than infection. Infectious causes like pyelonephritis typically present with steady pain and fever.

questions.text: A patient describes pain that starts in the flank and is felt continuously along the same dermatome down toward the groin, without appearing in an unrelated separate site. This pattern best describes which type of pain?
questions.explanation: Radiating pain is continuous along the extent of the same dermatome, unlike referred pain, which appears in two separate sites sharing a nerve root without continuity between them. Shifting pain instead moves entirely from one region to another over time.

questions.text: A patient reports that blood is noted only at the very beginning of urination and then the urine clears. Based on the timing of hematuria, where is the likely site of bleeding?
questions.explanation: Initial hematuria, where blood appears only at the start of urination before clearing, localizes the bleeding source to the urethra. Total hematuria throughout the stream instead suggests a bladder or upper tract origin.

questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with gross hematuria and passage of worm-shaped (vermiform) clots. This finding most strongly suggests bleeding originating from which site?
questions.explanation: Vermiform (worm-shaped) clots form as blood is molded within the narrow ureteric lumen, indicating an upper tract source. Clot presence in general signals a more significant degree of hematuria and higher likelihood of underlying pathology.

questions.text: A 65-year-old man presents with painless gross hematuria. What is the most common cause of gross hematuria in patients over age 50?
questions.explanation: Bladder cancer is the most common cause of gross hematuria in patients over 50 years old and must be excluded, as hematuria in adults is considered a symptom of malignancy until proven otherwise. Renal cell carcinoma is an important but less common differential.

questions.text: A patient reports waking up three times per night to urinate. How many nocturnal voids are considered clinically significant?
questions.explanation: Nocturia is defined as one or more rises from sleep to void, but it is only considered clinically significant when there are two or more episodes. Like frequency, it can result from increased urine output or decreased bladder capacity.

questions.text: A patient reports needing to use his abdominal muscles specifically during the terminal part of urination to complete voiding. This finding is best classified as which type of lower urinary tract symptom?
questions.explanation: Straining refers to the use of abdominal muscles to aid urination, normally used only at the end of voiding, and is classified as an obstructive/voiding symptom. This differs from irritative/storage symptoms such as frequency and urgency.

questions.text: A urologist is about to perform a complete physical examination on a male patient, including digital rectal examination (DRE). At what point in the examination sequence should the DRE be performed, and in what position?
options: First, in left lateral decubitus position
Last, in left lateral decubitus with knee-chest position
originalOptions: First, in left lateral decubitus position
Last, in left lateral decubitus with knee-chest position
questions.correctAnswer: C) Last, in left lateral decubitus with knee-chest position
questions.correctAnswerText: Last, in left lateral decubitus with knee-chest position
questions.explanation: DRE should be performed at the end of the physical examination, with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position with knees drawn to the chest. The examiner separates the buttocks to inspect the anus before gently inserting a lubricated finger to assess sphincter tone and palpate the prostate.

questions.text: A patient with suspected renal colic requires imaging to confirm the diagnosis. Which imaging modality is considered the gold standard for detecting urinary stones, and which modality would instead be preferred for staging prostate cancer?
options: MRI for stones; CT without contrast for prostate staging
Scrotal ultrasound for stones; bone scan for prostate staging
CT with contrast for stones; DMSA for prostate staging
CT without contrast for stones; MRI for prostate staging
Renal ultrasound for stones; micturating cystourethrogram for prostate staging
originalOptions: MRI for stones; CT without contrast for prostate staging
Scrotal ultrasound for stones; bone scan for prostate staging
CT with contrast for stones; DMSA for prostate staging
CT without contrast for stones; MRI for prostate staging
Renal ultrasound for stones; micturating cystourethrogram for prostate staging
questions.correctAnswer: D) CT without contrast for stones; MRI for prostate staging
questions.correctAnswerText: CT without contrast for stones; MRI for prostate staging
questions.explanation: Non-contrast CT is the gold standard for detecting urinary tract stones, while MRI is used for local staging of prostate cancer. Bone scan is reserved for detecting malignant prostate metastasis, not staging the primary tumor.

questions.text: On scrotal examination of an infertile male, both testes are palpable within the scrotum, but the vas deferens cannot be palpated bilaterally. This finding should raise suspicion for which underlying condition?
questions.explanation: Bilateral absence of the palpable vas deferens despite normally descended, palpable testes is classically associated with congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens, seen in cystic fibrosis. This is distinct from undescended testis, where the scrotum itself appears asymmetric and underdeveloped on one side.

questions.text: A patient has bone conduction better than air conduction on the right ear (negative Rinne). On Weber's test, sound is heard better in the right ear. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A negative Rinne test (bone conduction > air conduction) on the right ear indicates a conductive problem in that ear, and Weber lateralizing to the same (right) ear confirms this, since sound lateralizes toward the affected ear in conductive hearing loss. In sensorineural loss, Rinne would remain positive (air > bone) and Weber would lateralize to the opposite, better-hearing ear.

questions.text: A child presents with a midline neck lump that moves when they stick out their tongue. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A thyroglossal cyst is a midline neck lump that characteristically moves upward on tongue protrusion due to its embryological connection to the foramen cecum. Thyroid isthmus swelling moves with swallowing but not tongue protrusion, dermoid cysts are non-tender and mobile without this movement, and branchial cysts are lateral, not midline.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a cause of referred ear pain (otalgia)?
questions.explanation: Dental disease, TMJ dysfunction, and tonsillitis are all listed causes of referred (non-otological) ear pain. A scalp lipoma is a painless subcutaneous lump, not a source of referred otalgia.

questions.text: A heavy smoker presents with hoarseness of voice persisting for 3 weeks. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: Any smoker with hoarseness >3 weeks needs urgent fiberoptic laryngoscopy to rule out laryngeal tumor. Steroids, voice rest, or chest X-ray do not directly visualize the vocal cords and would delay this needed evaluation.

questions.text: Most common source of epistaxis:
questions.explanation: Kiesselbach's plexus (Little's area) on the anterior nasal septum is the most common site of epistaxis due to its rich, superficial vascular anastomosis. The other arteries contribute to this plexus or supply posterior/other regions but are not individually the most common source.

questions.text: Which of the following is a reason for urgent referral to ophthalmology?
questions.explanation: Chemical burns are true ocular emergencies requiring immediate irrigation for at least 30 minutes before any further workup, since delay risks irreversible ischemia to the eye. A, B, and D are chronic, non-urgent conditions that can be managed in routine follow-up, not urgent referral.

questions.text: The neural part of the eye is the:
questions.explanation: The retina forms the neural layer of the eye, containing photoreceptors and neurons. Cornea and sclera are part of the fibrous layer, while the lens is a refractive structure, not neural tissue.

questions.text: Which of the following is part of a routine pupil examination?
questions.explanation: Active light testing (pupillary light response) evaluates how the pupils constrict and dilate in response to light, making it the core component of a pupil examination. While slit-lamp biomicroscopy inspects the overall structure of the eye, tests like fluorescein angiography and optical coherence tomography (OCT) are advanced imaging techniques for the retina and blood vessels, not part of a standard pupil evaluation.

questions.text: Contact lens users are at increased risk for:
questions.explanation: Contact lens wear increases risk of microbial keratitis due to corneal surface disruption and contamination. Cataract, glaucoma, and pterygium are not specifically linked to contact lens use.

questions.text: Red eye serious symptom:
questions.explanation: Photophobia suggests corneal or intraocular involvement (e.g., keratitis, uveitis), making it a red flag symptom. Watery discharge and itching point to allergic/viral conjunctivitis, and foreign body sensation is less specific for serious pathology.

allQuestions.text: Which layer of the epidermis serves as the site of origin for new keratinocytes that subsequently migrate upward through the epidermis?
allQuestions.explanation: The stratum basale is the deepest epidermal layer where keratinocytes proliferate before migrating upward through the spinosum, granulosum, and corneum. The other layers represent later stages of keratinocyte maturation, not sites of origin. The papillary dermis is a dermal, not epidermal, structure.

allQuestions.text: A 24-year-old presents with a solid, elevated skin lesion measuring 0.4 cm in diameter with no depth into the dermis. What is the most accurate term for this lesion?
allQuestions.explanation: A papule is a solid, elevated lesion less than 0.5 cm in diameter. Nodules are larger and extend deeper into the dermis, while plaques exceed 0.5 cm and are typically formed by confluent papules. Macules are flat, not elevated, ruling that option out.

allQuestions.text: Allergic contact dermatitis is best classified as which type of hypersensitivity reaction, and which bedside test is used to confirm it?
options: Type I hypersensitivity; confirmed by prick testing
Type II hypersensitivity; confirmed by skin biopsy
Type IV hypersensitivity; confirmed by patch testing
Type III hypersensitivity; confirmed by Tzanck smear
Type I hypersensitivity; confirmed by Wood's lamp
originalOptions: Type I hypersensitivity; confirmed by prick testing
Type II hypersensitivity; confirmed by skin biopsy
Type IV hypersensitivity; confirmed by patch testing
Type III hypersensitivity; confirmed by Tzanck smear
Type I hypersensitivity; confirmed by Wood's lamp
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Type IV hypersensitivity; confirmed by patch testing
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Type IV hypersensitivity; confirmed by patch testing
allQuestions.explanation: Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed (Type IV) hypersensitivity reaction, confirmed with patch testing where allergens are applied under occlusion for 48 hours and read later. Prick testing instead evaluates immediate (Type I) reactions such as classic allergies, making it inappropriate here.

allQuestions.text: A patient has a superficial skin lesion caused by loss of the epidermis only, which is expected to heal without scarring. What is this lesion called?
allQuestions.explanation: Erosion involves loss limited to the epidermis and heals without scarring, whereas an ulcer extends into the dermis and heals with scarring. Fissures are linear cracks rather than areas of tissue loss, and atrophy refers to thinning, not loss, of skin layers.

allQuestions.text: A patient with chronic eczema who reports years of persistent scratching now has thickened skin with exaggerated skin markings over the affected area. What secondary skin change does this describe?
allQuestions.explanation: Lichenification is thickening of the skin with accentuated markings resulting from chronic rubbing or scratching, classically seen in long-standing eczema. Atrophy describes thinning rather than thickening, making it the opposite finding.

allQuestions.text: On Wood's lamp examination in a darkened room, a depigmented patch of skin appears chalky white. This finding is most consistent with which condition?
allQuestions.explanation: Vitiligo, a condition of complete depigmentation, produces a characteristic chalky white fluorescence under Wood's lamp, distinguishing it from hypopigmented conditions like pityriasis alba, which appear pale rather than chalky white. Tinea capitis and erythrasma instead produce green and coral pink fluorescence, respectively, reflecting infectious rather than pigmentary causes.

allQuestions.text: Skin scrapings from a scaly plaque are treated with potassium hydroxide to dissolve keratin prior to microscopic examination. This bedside test is primarily used to identify which type of infection?
allQuestions.explanation: KOH preparation dissolves keratin to allow visualization of fungal hyphae and spores, making it the standard bedside test for suspected fungal infections. Viral infections are instead assessed with a Tzanck smear, which detects multinucleated giant cells rather than fungal elements.

allQuestions.text: A flat, circumscribed area of discoloration measuring 0.6 cm in diameter is noted on examination, with no elevation or palpable substance. How should this lesion be classified?
allQuestions.explanation: A macule is a flat, circumscribed discoloration less than 1 cm in diameter, fitting this 0.6 cm lesion. A patch describes the same flat morphology but only when greater than 1 cm, while papules and plaques are by definition elevated, not flat.

allQuestions.text: What is the wavelength of ultraviolet light emitted by a Wood's lamp used in dermatological examination?
allQuestions.explanation: The Wood's lamp emits UVA light at approximately 365 nm, used to elicit characteristic fluorescence patterns in various infectious and pigmentary skin conditions. UVB and UVC wavelengths are not used for this purpose in standard dermatological bedside testing.

allQuestions.text: All of the following fluorescence colors on Wood's lamp examination are correctly matched with their causative condition EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Vitiligo characteristically shows a chalky white appearance under Wood's lamp due to complete depigmentation, not golden yellow fluorescence. Golden yellow fluorescence is instead the classic finding in pityriasis versicolor, an infectious rather than pigmentary condition.

allQuestions.text: A young male presents with unilateral epistaxis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
allQuestions.explanation: Unilateral epistaxis in a young male (adolescent) is a classic presentation of juvenile nasal angiofibroma (JNA), a vascular tumor requiring rule-out by nasal endoscopy. Septal deviation and foreign body typically cause obstruction rather than recurrent bleeding, and allergic rhinitis/nasal polyps are usually bilateral.

allQuestions.text: A patient has bone conduction better than air conduction on the right ear (negative Rinne). On Weber's test, sound is heard better in the right ear. What is the diagnosis?
allQuestions.explanation: A negative Rinne test (bone conduction > air conduction) on the right ear indicates a conductive problem in that ear, and Weber lateralizing to the same (right) ear confirms this, since sound lateralizes toward the affected ear in conductive hearing loss. In sensorineural loss, Rinne would remain positive (air > bone) and Weber would lateralize to the opposite, better-hearing ear.

allQuestions.text: What tuning fork frequency is used for hearing tests?
allQuestions.explanation: The standard tuning fork used for Weber's and Rinne's tests is 512 Hz, providing a balance between adequate duration of vibration and clinical accuracy. Lower frequencies (128–256 Hz) are felt more than heard, while higher frequencies decay too quickly for reliable bedside testing.

allQuestions.text: A child presents with a midline neck lump that moves when they stick out their tongue. What is the diagnosis?
allQuestions.explanation: A thyroglossal cyst is a midline neck lump that characteristically moves upward on tongue protrusion due to its embryological connection to the foramen cecum. Thyroid isthmus swelling moves with swallowing but not tongue protrusion, dermoid cysts are non-tender and mobile without this movement, and branchial cysts are lateral, not midline.

allQuestions.text: A 55-year-old male smoker presents with hoarseness of voice persisting for 3 weeks. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Urgent referral to ENT for fiberoptic laryngoscopy
originalOptions: Urgent referral to ENT for fiberoptic laryngoscopy
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Urgent referral to ENT for fiberoptic laryngoscopy
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Urgent referral to ENT for fiberoptic laryngoscopy
allQuestions.explanation: Any smoker with hoarseness lasting more than 3 weeks is a red flag requiring urgent ENT referral for fiberoptic endoscopy to look for laryngeal tumors, as emphasized directly in the lecture. Antibiotics, PPIs, or reassurance risk delaying diagnosis of a potentially malignant cause.

allQuestions.text: A young male teacher presents with hoarseness of voice for 3 weeks with a history of prolonged vocal strain. Laryngoscopy reveals a smooth, unilateral lesion on the vocal cord. What is the most likely diagnosis?
allQuestions.explanation: A vocal cord polyp typically presents as a unilateral, smooth lesion following a single episode of vocal strain or trauma, unlike nodules which are bilateral and related to chronic voice abuse (e.g., singers/teachers using their voice repetitively).

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a cause of referred ear pain (otalgia)?
allQuestions.explanation: Dental disease, TMJ dysfunction, and tonsillitis are all listed causes of referred (non-otological) ear pain. A scalp lipoma is a painless subcutaneous lump, not a source of referred otalgia.

allQuestions.text: A heavy smoker presents with hoarseness of voice persisting for 3 weeks. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

allQuestions.text: A patient arrives at the emergency department with wheezing and a history of asthma. In the triage process, you need to categorize the patient and determine the initial position or intervention. Given the patient's condition, which of the following is the most appropriate triage category and initial action?
options: Green (Minimal) - Have the patient lie flat and provide bronchodilators at a later time.
Red (Immediate) - Place the patient in an upright position and administer bronchodilators immediately.
Black (Deceased) - No intervention required, prioritize other patients.
Yellow (Delayed) - Place the patient in a semi-reclining position and administer bronchodilators as soon as possible.
Not classified - Refer the patient directly to an outpatient clinic without triage.
originalOptions: Green (Minimal) - Have the patient lie flat and provide bronchodilators at a later time.
Red (Immediate) - Place the patient in an upright position and administer bronchodilators immediately.

Yellow (Delayed) - Place the patient in a semi-reclining position and administer bronchodilators as soon as possible.

allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Yellow (Delayed) - Place the patient in a semi-reclining position and administer bronchodilators as soon as possible.
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Yellow (Delayed) - Place the patient in a semi-reclining position and administer bronchodilators as soon as possible.
allQuestions.explanation: A wheezing asthmatic without signs of severe respiratory failure is not yet at ESI Level 1/Red, but still requires prompt care, placing them in the Yellow/urgent range. A semi-reclining position eases work of breathing, unlike lying flat (Green), which would worsen dyspnea. Red is reserved for patients in profound distress or actively dying.

allQuestions.text: A patient arrives at the emergency department with a capillary refill time greater than 3 seconds. In the triage process, which of the following is the most appropriate triage category and initial action?
options: Yellow (Delayed) - Place the patient in a semi-reclining position and monitor closely before further action.
Red (Immediate) - Assess the patient urgently and initiate immediate resuscitation and stabilization.
Green (Minimal) - Have the patient sit comfortably and provide non-urgent care at a later time.
Not classified - Delay assessment until vital signs are formally documented.
originalOptions: Yellow (Delayed) - Place the patient in a semi-reclining position and monitor closely before further action.
Red (Immediate) - Assess the patient urgently and initiate immediate resuscitation and stabilization.
Green (Minimal) - Have the patient sit comfortably and provide non-urgent care at a later time.
Not classified - Delay assessment until vital signs are formally documented.
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Red (Immediate) - Assess the patient urgently and initiate immediate resuscitation and stabilization.
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Red (Immediate) - Assess the patient urgently and initiate immediate resuscitation and stabilization.
allQuestions.explanation: A capillary refill greater than 3 seconds signals poor peripheral perfusion and possible shock, a time-critical finding requiring immediate resuscitation, consistent with ESI Level 1/Red. Yellow or Green categories underestimate the danger of impending hemodynamic collapse, while Black applies only to patients who are deceased, not those who are still salvageable.

allQuestions.text: What is the primary purpose of assigning a triage category to a patient?
options: To prioritize the patient's care based on the level of urgency
To establish the patient's demographic information for hospital records
To determine the patient's previous medical conditions before treatment begins
To evaluate the patient's insurance coverage prior to admission
To assign the patient to a specific physician based on specialty preference
originalOptions: To prioritize the patient's care based on the level of urgency
To establish the patient's demographic information for hospital records
To determine the patient's previous medical conditions before treatment begins
To evaluate the patient's insurance coverage prior to admission
To assign the patient to a specific physician based on specialty preference
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) To prioritize the patient's care based on the level of urgency
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: To prioritize the patient's care based on the level of urgency
allQuestions.explanation: Triage exists to sort patients by medical acuity so the sickest are seen first, reflecting the ED principle that care is not given on a first-come, first-served basis. Demographic data, insurance status, and physician assignment are administrative functions and play no role in the acuity-based sorting that defines triage.

allQuestions.text: A 60-year-old male is brought to the ED. On assessment, his respiratory rate is 34/min, capillary refill time is 4 seconds, and he is unable to follow simple commands. What is the most appropriate triage category for this patient?
allQuestions.explanation: RR > 30/min and capillary refill > 3 seconds are signs of shock, and combined with an altered ability to follow commands, this patient is critically unstable. Any patient in shock requires immediate resuscitation and is placed in the Red area regardless of the specific diagnosis.

allQuestions.text: A 33-year-old female with a known history of asthma presents with difficulty breathing and wheezing for 3 days. She is able to speak in full, understandable sentences but must pause periodically to catch her breath. She is not in cardiac or respiratory arrest. What is the most appropriate triage category?
allQuestions.explanation: Because she can still speak in full sentences, she does not meet resuscitation criteria and is taken out of the Red area. However, she still has objective difficulty breathing and requires active management, so she cannot be classified as low-acuity — placing her in the Yellow area.

allQuestions.text: A 33-year-old female with a known history of asthma presents to the ED with a silent chest and is unable to speak in full sentences due to severe respiratory distress. What is the most appropriate triage category for this patient?
options: Discharge home with a rescue inhaler
originalOptions: Discharge home with a rescue inhaler
allQuestions.explanation: A silent chest and inability to speak in full sentences indicate impending or actual respiratory failure. This patient is critically unstable and requires immediate resuscitation, placing her in the Red area — the same category used for cardiac/respiratory arrest and any patient who "cannot be left" without immediate intervention.

allQuestions.text: According to the described signs of respiratory distress in a critically ill patient requiring an immediate response, all of the following are correct EXCEPT:
options: Use of accessory muscles is a warning sign
Tachypnea (very fast breathing) is a warning sign
A patient may progress to confusion or drowsiness due to respiratory muscle fatigue
CO2 retention leading to drowsiness is especially concerning in COPD patients
Bradypnea with fully normal mentation is the expected pattern of deterioration
originalOptions: Use of accessory muscles is a warning sign
Tachypnea (very fast breathing) is a warning sign
A patient may progress to confusion or drowsiness due to respiratory muscle fatigue
CO2 retention leading to drowsiness is especially concerning in COPD patients
Bradypnea with fully normal mentation is the expected pattern of deterioration
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Bradypnea with fully normal mentation is the expected pattern of deterioration
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Bradypnea with fully normal mentation is the expected pattern of deterioration
allQuestions.explanation: The described pattern of deterioration is accessory muscle use → tachypnea → confusion/drowsiness from respiratory muscle fatigue and CO2 retention, which is particularly dangerous in COPD patients. A calm, fully alert patient with slow breathing does not reflect this warning pattern — drowsiness/confusion is the expected finding, not normal mentation.

allQuestions.text: A patient arrives at the ED due to toxin exposure or ingestion of a liquid cleaning agent. He currently appears well and is talking normally. What is the appropriate triage category for this patient?
options: Red area, regardless of his current general appearance
Yellow area, since he currently looks stable
Green area, since no obvious distress is present
Triage should be based only on his current vital signs
He can be observed briefly in the waiting area before triage

Yellow area, since he currently looks stable
Green area, since no obvious distress is present
Triage should be based only on his current vital signs
He can be observed briefly in the waiting area before triage
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Red area, regardless of his current general appearance
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Red area, regardless of his current general appearance
allQuestions.explanation: Any patient exposed to toxins or who has ingested a toxic substance is placed in the Red area regardless of how well they currently appear, because such patients may deteriorate suddenly and become critically ill at any time.

allQuestions.text: A patient in the ED is found to be pulseless. What is the immediate and correct course of action?
options: Assess the ABCs fully before deciding on any action
Wait for the triage nurse to formally confirm pulselessness before acting
Call for help and immediately start CPR; the patient is classified as Red area
Move the patient to the Yellow area pending further assessment
Discharge the patient if no pulse is felt after a brief check
originalOptions: Assess the ABCs fully before deciding on any action
Wait for the triage nurse to formally confirm pulselessness before acting
Call for help and immediately start CPR; the patient is classified as Red area
Move the patient to the Yellow area pending further assessment

allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Call for help and immediately start CPR; the patient is classified as Red area
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Call for help and immediately start CPR; the patient is classified as Red area
allQuestions.explanation: Any pulseless patient requires an immediate call for help and initiation of CPR without delay. This is an automatic Red area (resuscitation) classification, as the patient needs immediate life-saving intervention.

allQuestions.text: A trauma patient arrives at the ED. Which of the following is NOT considered a high-risk mechanism of injury requiring trauma team activation?
options: Fall from twice the patient's height
Penetrating trauma proximal to the knee/elbow, with bleeding controlled
originalOptions: Fall from twice the patient's height
Penetrating trauma proximal to the knee/elbow, with bleeding controlled
allQuestions.explanation: Fall from twice the patient's height, penetrating trauma proximal to the knee/elbow (with bleeding controlled), crush injury, and pedestrian-vehicle collisions are all recognized high-risk mechanisms that mandate a high level of trauma concern regardless of the patient's initial appearance. An isolated femur fracture, while serious, is a specific injury rather than a high-risk mechanism criterion.

allQuestions.text: A patient with full decision-making capacity refuses a proposed treatment after being informed of the risks and benefits. Which ethical principle does the physician's obligation to respect this refusal reflect?
allQuestions.explanation: Autonomy is the ethical principle granting a competent patient the right to accept or refuse medical treatment, even if that refusal may lead to a poor outcome. The physician must honor this right as long as the patient has intact decision-making capacity.

allQuestions.text: A physician fully and honestly discloses a patient's diagnosis and prognosis to them, even when the news is difficult. This practice of truth-telling is grounded in which ethical principle?
allQuestions.explanation: Truth-telling is a component of respecting patient autonomy, since a patient cannot exercise informed decision-making or give valid informed consent without accurate and honest information about their condition.

allQuestions.text: During a difficult conversation with a distressed patient, a physician actively listens and seeks to understand the root cause of the patient's distress rather than immediately offering solutions. What communication skill is being demonstrated?
allQuestions.explanation: Active listening involves fully attending to the patient, seeking to understand the underlying source of their distress rather than reacting superficially. This builds trust and allows the physician to address the patient's actual concerns, which is essential to effective doctor-patient communication.

allQuestions.text: A patient with an acute surgical emergency and intact decision-making capacity refuses a life-saving surgery after being informed of the consequences of refusal, including death. What should the physician do?
options: Perform the surgery regardless, since it is life-saving
Obtain a court order to override the patient's decision immediately
Sedate the patient and proceed with surgery
Respect the patient's refusal, since autonomy permits refusal even of life-saving treatment
Ignore the refusal and proceed once family consents instead

Respect the patient's refusal, since autonomy permits refusal even of life-saving treatment

allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Respect the patient's refusal, since autonomy permits refusal even of life-saving treatment
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Respect the patient's refusal, since autonomy permits refusal even of life-saving treatment
allQuestions.explanation: A competent, informed patient has the right to refuse even life-saving treatment under the principle of autonomy. The physician must document that the patient had capacity, was informed of the risks (including death), and still chose to refuse.

allQuestions.text: In the emergency department, patients are treated according to which of the following principles?
options: Order of insurance or payment status
Priority based on the severity of their condition
Random allocation to balance departmental workload
originalOptions: Order of insurance or payment status
Priority based on the severity of their condition
Random allocation to balance departmental workload
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Priority based on the severity of their condition
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Priority based on the severity of their condition
allQuestions.explanation: Unlike most other settings, ED patients are not seen on a first-come, first-served basis. Triage ensures that patients are treated according to the severity and urgency of their condition, so that the most critically ill receive care first.

allQuestions.text: What is the correct sequence of steps in basic life support (BLS) upon encountering an unresponsive patient?
options: Call 911 → Tap and shout → Check for breathing → Chest compressions
Tap and shout → Call 911 → Check for breathing → Chest compressions
Check for breathing → Tap and shout → Chest compressions → Call 911
Chest compressions → Tap and shout → Call 911 → Check for breathing
Tap and shout → Check for breathing → Call 911 → Chest compressions

Check for breathing → Tap and shout → Chest compressions → Call 911
Chest compressions → Tap and shout → Call 911 → Check for breathing
Tap and shout → Check for breathing → Call 911 → Chest compressions
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Tap and shout → Call 911 → Check for breathing → Chest compressions
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Tap and shout → Call 911 → Check for breathing → Chest compressions
allQuestions.explanation: The correct BLS sequence begins with assessing responsiveness (tap and shout), then activating emergency services (call 911), followed by checking for breathing, and finally starting chest compressions if the patient is not breathing normally. Following this order ensures help is on the way before proceeding with further steps.

allQuestions.text: What is the primary purpose of performing high-quality, early CPR in a patient in cardiac arrest?
options: To restore normal heart rhythm directly

To reduce the need for advanced airway management
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) To prevent irreversible brain damage by maintaining perfusion
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: To prevent irreversible brain damage by maintaining perfusion
allQuestions.explanation: The brain is extremely sensitive to oxygen deprivation. High-quality CPR maintains circulation and oxygen delivery to vital organs, most critically the brain, until spontaneous circulation returns or definitive treatment (such as defibrillation) can be administered. Delaying CPR risks irreversible neurological injury.

allQuestions.text: While explaining a poor prognosis to a patient, the patient's brother becomes angry, begins shouting, and behaves aggressively toward you. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Continue the conversation calmly and ignore the aggressive behavior
Raise your voice to regain control of the conversation
Ask the patient to calm their brother down
Leave the room if your safety is at risk, and call security
Sedate the brother to de-escalate the situation

allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Leave the room if your safety is at risk, and call security
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Leave the room if your safety is at risk, and call security

allQuestions.text: At what age should osteoporosis screening begin routinely, and at what age in high-risk patients?
options: Age 50 routinely; age 45 in high-risk patients
Age 60 routinely; age 50 in high-risk patients
Age 70 routinely; age 65 in high-risk patients
Age 65 routinely; age 60 in high-risk patients
Age 55 routinely; age 50 in high-risk patients

Age 55 routinely; age 50 in high-risk patients
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Age 65 routinely; age 60 in high-risk patients
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Age 65 routinely; age 60 in high-risk patients
allQuestions.explanation: Routine osteoporosis screening begins at age 65 in average-risk individuals, but is moved earlier to age 60 in patients with risk factors such as low body weight or family history. The other age pairs are close distractors but do not match the standard screening thresholds.

allQuestions.text: At what age should hyperlipidemia screening begin in men with no risk factors?
options: Men aged 45 and older, regardless of risk factors
Men aged 35 and older, regardless of risk factors

allQuestions.text: Which of the following statements about the role of a general practitioner is incorrect?
options: The role of a general practitioner does not include focusing on preventive measures or interventions.
The general practitioner is a licensed medical graduate who provides care to individuals regardless of age, sex, and illness.
The general practitioner aims to make early diagnoses and may attend to patients in various settings, including their homes, consulting rooms, clinics, or hospitals.

allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The role of a general practitioner does not include focusing on preventive measures or interventions.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a criterion for diagnosing metabolic syndrome?
options: Waist circumference greater than 35 inches (89 cm) in women and 40 inches in men
Triglyceride levels of 150 milligrams per deciliter (mg/dl) or higher
Blood pressure of 130/85 millimeters of mercury or higher
Fasting blood glucose level of 110 mg/dl or higher
High-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL) lower than 60 milligrams per deciliter (mg/dl)

allQuestions.explanation: The actual HDL criterion for metabolic syndrome is a low HDL (below approximately 40 mg/dl in men or 50 mg/dl in women), not "lower than 60," so this threshold is incorrect and does not represent a true diagnostic criterion. Waist circumference, triglycerides, blood pressure, and fasting glucose thresholds listed in the other options are all accurate components of the diagnosis.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following correctly represents the abbreviation for "E" in the context of RISE?
allQuestions.explanation: In the RISE framework, "E" stands for Education/Counseling, reflecting the physician's role in patient education as part of comprehensive care. The other options describe plausible-sounding but incorrect expansions of the letter.

allQuestions.text: If a patient has a visual acuity of 6/12, what does this mean?
options: They can see at 6 meters what a person with normal vision can see at 12 meters
They can see at 12 meters what a person with normal vision can see at 6 meters
Their vision is better than normal, resolving details invisible to the average eye at 6 meters
They have normal visual acuity equivalent to 6/6
They can only perceive hand movements at a distance of 6 meters
originalOptions: They can see at 6 meters what a person with normal vision can see at 12 meters
They can see at 12 meters what a person with normal vision can see at 6 meters
Their vision is better than normal, resolving details invisible to the average eye at 6 meters
They have normal visual acuity equivalent to 6/6
They can only perceive hand movements at a distance of 6 meters
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) They can see at 6 meters what a person with normal vision can see at 12 meters
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: They can see at 6 meters what a person with normal vision can see at 12 meters
allQuestions.explanation: 6/12 = test distance/normal distance, meaning reduced acuity, not enhanced. B reverses the fraction (would mean better-than-normal vision), C and D wrongly describe normal or supranormal vision, and E describes near-blindness, far worse than 6/12.

allQuestions.text: This test is used to asses ? [img: colorvision.png]
allQuestions.explanation: This is an Ishihara pseudoisochromatic plate, used specifically for color vision testing. A uses the Snellen chart, B uses a light source, C uses confrontation/perimetry, and E uses contrast charts — none use colored dot plates.

allQuestions.text: What condition causes acute painful loss of vision?
allQuestions.explanation: Only angle-closure glaucoma is both acute and painful. A and E are acute but painless, while C and D are painless and gradual, not acute.

allQuestions.text: All are causes of this sign except ? [img: redeye.png]
allQuestions.explanation: Macular edema is a retinal/central vision problem, not a cause of ocular redness. A–D all directly cause a red eye through conjunctival, corneal, or intraocular inflammation/hemorrhage.

allQuestions.text: What is the term for pupils of different sizes?
allQuestions.explanation: Anisocoria specifically means unequal pupil size. Nystagmus is involuntary eye movement, ptosis is lid drooping, diplopia is double vision, and RAPD is an abnormal light reflex — none describe pupil size difference.

allQuestions.text: What is the visual field exam called?
allQuestions.explanation: The confrontation test is the bedside visual field exam. A tests color, B tests for RAPD, D tests acuity, and E examines the fundus — all test different functions.

allQuestions.text: What are the three components involved in accommodation?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Accommodation, pupillary constriction, and convergence
allQuestions.explanation: The near reflex triad is lens accommodation + pupillary constriction + convergence. B and C swap in divergence (the opposite of convergence), D swaps in dilation (opposite of constriction), and E replaces accommodation with visual acuity, which isn't part of the triad.

allQuestions.text: The limbus houses germinative stem cells that maintain the corneal epithelium. What is the primary function of this layer?
options: Anchoring the epithelium via desmosomes only
Providing mechanical strength via collagen fibrils
Regeneration and proliferation of epithelial cells
originalOptions: Anchoring the epithelium via desmosomes only
Providing mechanical strength via collagen fibrils
Regeneration and proliferation of epithelial cells
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Regeneration and proliferation of epithelial cells
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Regeneration and proliferation of epithelial cells
allQuestions.explanation: Limbal stem cells continuously regenerate the corneal epithelium, allowing rapid repair after abrasion by cell spreading and proliferation. A is incomplete, as anchoring also involves hemidesmosomes and fibrils, not desmosomes alone. B is wrong — the endothelium instead repairs by cell spreading alone with loss of density, no regeneration. C and D describe Bowman's layer and the trabecular meshwork, unrelated structures.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a reason for urgent referral to ophthalmology?
allQuestions.explanation: Chemical burns are true ocular emergencies requiring immediate irrigation for at least 30 minutes before any further workup, since delay risks irreversible ischemia to the eye. A, B, and D are chronic, non-urgent conditions that can be managed in routine follow-up, not urgent referral.

allQuestions.text: The neural part of the eye is the:
allQuestions.explanation: The retina forms the neural layer of the eye, containing photoreceptors and neurons. Cornea and sclera are part of the fibrous layer, while the lens is a refractive structure, not neural tissue.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is part of a routine pupil examination?
allQuestions.explanation: Active light testing (pupillary light response) evaluates how the pupils constrict and dilate in response to light, making it the core component of a pupil examination. While slit-lamp biomicroscopy inspects the overall structure of the eye, tests like fluorescein angiography and optical coherence tomography (OCT) are advanced imaging techniques for the retina and blood vessels, not part of a standard pupil evaluation.

allQuestions.text: Contact lens users are at increased risk for:
allQuestions.explanation: Contact lens wear increases risk of microbial keratitis due to corneal surface disruption and contamination. Cataract, glaucoma, and pterygium are not specifically linked to contact lens use.

allQuestions.text: Red eye serious symptom:
allQuestions.explanation: Photophobia suggests corneal or intraocular involvement (e.g., keratitis, uveitis), making it a red flag symptom. Watery discharge and itching point to allergic/viral conjunctivitis, and foreign body sensation is less specific for serious pathology.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a sign of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)?
allQuestions.explanation: BPH causes obstructive LUTS such as hesitancy, poor stream, straining, and incomplete emptying due to bladder outlet obstruction. Dysuria (painful urination) reflects inflammation/infection rather than mechanical obstruction, so it is not a typical BPH sign.

allQuestions.text: What is the most likely cause of continuous urinary incontinence?
allQuestions.explanation: A vesicovaginal fistula creates an abnormal communication between the bladder and vagina, causing continuous, position-independent urine leakage. Stress and urge incontinence are intermittent and related to activity or sudden urge, not constant leakage.

allQuestions.text: All of the following can cause pneumaturia EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Pneumaturia (gas in urine) results from recent catheterization, enteric fistulas communicating with the urinary tract, or infection with gas-forming organisms. An ectopic ureter causes abnormal ureteral insertion and incontinence, not gas in the urine.

allQuestions.text: Choose the conditions that cause urine to appear cloudy: (Select all that apply)
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Pyuria / B) Phosphaturia / D) Chyluria
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: A) Pyuria / B) Phosphaturia / D) Chyluria
allQuestions.explanation: Pyuria causes turbidity from WBCs/pus, phosphaturia from phosphate crystal precipitation in alkaline urine (classic post-meal benign cause), and chyluria from lymphatic fluid mixing with urine. If a single option is required by the question, B is selected because pyuria and chyluria change urine turbidity too, while phosphaturia remains the classic non-pathological textbook answer for cloudiness. Hematuria and bilirubinuria mainly change urine color (red/dark amber) rather than causing true cloudiness.

allQuestions.text: Hematuria can best be distinguished from hemoglobinuria or myoglobinuria by which of the following?
allQuestions.explanation: Dipstick testing is positive for blood in all three conditions since it detects heme, but only true hematuria shows intact RBCs on microscopic sediment analysis. Hemoglobinuria and myoglobinuria show a positive dipstick with no RBCs seen microscopically.

allQuestions.text: What is the most common cause of glomerular hematuria?
allQuestions.explanation: IgA nephropathy is the most common cause of glomerular hematuria worldwide, often presenting with episodic gross hematuria following upper respiratory infections. The other options are important but less common causes of glomerular bleeding.

allQuestions.text: What is the underlying cause of pain associated with ureteral stones?
options: Direct mechanical nerve compression by the stone
originalOptions: Direct mechanical nerve compression by the stone
allQuestions.explanation: Ureteral colic results from acute obstruction causing distension and spasm of the ureteral wall proximal to the stone, producing fluctuating, colicky pain. This differs from steady inflammatory pain, which is caused by capsular distension rather than obstruction.

allQuestions.text: A Tzanck smear performed on scrapings from the base of a vesicle reveals multinucleated giant cells. This finding is most consistent with which infection?
allQuestions.explanation: Multinucleated giant cells on Tzanck smear are the classic finding in herpes simplex and varicella zoster infections. Acantholytic cells, not multinucleated giant cells, are the characteristic finding in pemphigus.

allQuestions.text: Which investigation involves introducing allergen into the skin and assessing for a wheal-and-flare reaction within 10-15 minutes?
allQuestions.explanation: Prick testing evaluates immediate Type I hypersensitivity by introducing allergen into the skin and observing wheal formation within 10-15 minutes. Patch testing instead assesses delayed Type IV reactions over 48 hours.

allQuestions.text: Which dermal cell type is primarily responsible for synthesizing collagen, elastin, and other extracellular matrix components?
allQuestions.explanation: Fibroblasts synthesize collagen, elastin, glycosaminoglycans, and other extracellular matrix components that give the dermis its structural support. Mast cells and macrophages instead contribute to inflammatory and immune functions.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with pinpoint, non-blanchable hemorrhagic lesions measuring less than 3 mm in diameter. What is the appropriate term for these lesions?
allQuestions.explanation: Petechiae are pinpoint, non-blanchable hemorrhages less than 3 mm, often indicating platelet abnormalities or vasculopathy. Purpura and ecchymosis describe larger hemorrhagic lesions, 3-10 mm and greater than 10 mm respectively.

allQuestions.text: Which clinical sign, characterized by pinpoint bleeding upon removal of overlying scale, is classically associated with a papulosquamous condition featuring well-defined plaques on extensor surfaces?
allQuestions.explanation: The Auspitz sign, pinpoint bleeding after scale removal, is a special feature of psoriasis, which presents with well-defined, silvery-scaled plaques on extensor surfaces. Wickham's striae instead refer to fine white lines seen in lichen planus.

allQuestions.text: Purple, polygonal, pruritic papules and plaques with fine white lines on their surface, commonly affecting the wrists and oral mucosa, are associated with which named surface finding?
allQuestions.explanation: Wickham's striae are fine white lines seen on the surface of lichen planus papules, a helpful diagnostic feature alongside the classic purple, polygonal, pruritic morphology. The Auspitz sign, by contrast, is specific to psoriasis rather than lichen planus.

allQuestions.text: A generalized papulosquamous eruption preceded by a single larger lesion, followed by a distribution along skin lines on the trunk, is most consistent with which condition?
allQuestions.explanation: Pityriasis rosea characteristically begins with a herald patch followed by a generalized eruption oriented along skin lines, producing a "Christmas tree" pattern on the trunk. Psoriasis instead favors extensor surfaces with well-defined, silvery plaques rather than a herald patch.

allQuestions.text: A red lesion does not fade when compressed with a glass slide. This negative diascopy result is most consistent with which underlying process?
allQuestions.explanation: Non-blanchable redness on diascopy indicates hemorrhage with extravasated blood outside the vasculature, as seen in purpura or petechiae. Blanchable lesions such as urticaria and telangiectasia result from vasodilation rather than hemorrhage.

allQuestions.text: Patch testing for suspected allergic contact dermatitis involves applying allergens under occlusion to the skin for how long before the initial reading?
allQuestions.explanation: Patch testing requires allergens to remain under occlusion on the skin for 48 hours, with reactions reassessed later at 72-96 hours. This delayed timeline reflects the Type IV hypersensitivity mechanism being tested, unlike the rapid 10-15 minute readout of prick testing.

allQuestions.text: Which epidermal layer is composed mainly of lipids and functions as the primary barrier preventing penetration of harmful substances and moisture loss
allQuestions.explanation: The stratum corneum is the outermost, dead, lipid-rich layer that serves as the skin's principal barrier against harmful substances and moisture loss. The stratum basale, by contrast, is the deepest proliferative layer rather than the barrier layer.

allQuestions.text: Damage to desmosomal connections between keratinocytes, as seen in pemphigus, results in which histological finding?
allQuestions.explanation: Desmosomes maintain keratinocyte adhesion, and their disruption produces acantholysis, the loss of cell-to-cell cohesion characteristic of pemphigus. This differs from hyperkeratosis, which reflects excess stratum corneum thickening rather than loss of adhesion.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with red, non-blanchable, palpable lesions on the legs that are painful and have persisted for several weeks. Which condition is most likely?
allQuestions.explanation: Vasculitis classically presents as palpable, non-blanchable purpura on the legs, often painful and persisting for weeks, reflecting a hemorrhagic rather than vasodilatory process. Urticaria, in contrast, is blanchable and transient, resolving within hours.

allQuestions.text: A skin defect extending through the epidermis and into at least part of the dermis, expected to heal with scar formation, is best classified as which lesion?
allQuestions.explanation: An ulcer involves loss of epidermis and at least part of the dermis, and therefore heals with scarring. An erosion is limited to the epidermis alone and heals without scarring, distinguishing it from an ulcer.

allQuestions.text: Which feature most reliably distinguishes eczema from psoriasis on clinical examination?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Ill-defined margins versus well-defined margins
allQuestions.explanation: Eczema classically has ill-defined margins, whereas psoriasis presents with sharply well-defined plaque margins, making margin definition a key distinguishing feature. Scale, erythema, and pruritus can occur in both conditions and are therefore less discriminating.

allQuestions.text: Linear, curvilinear tracks in the epidermis produced by a burrowing organism are known as which special skin lesion, and are diagnostic of which condition?
allQuestions.explanation: Burrows are linear or curvilinear tracts created by burrowing mites and are diagnostic for scabies infestation. Fissures, by contrast, are linear cracks caused by mechanical splitting rather than parasitic burrowing.

allQuestions.text: Which level of prehospital care provider is trained to perform endotracheal intubation, establish IV access, and administer a wide range of emergency medications?
allQuestions.explanation: Paramedics provide Advanced Life Support (ALS), including intubation, IV access, cardiac monitoring, and administration of emergency drugs. EMRs and EMTs are limited to basic interventions like CPR, bleeding control, and non-invasive airway management. Critical Care Transport teams handle complex inter-facility transfers, not initial field ALS care.

allQuestions.text: A patient arrives unresponsive with severe respiratory distress and profound shock. According to the Emergency Severity Index, which triage level should this patient receive?
allQuestions.explanation: ESI Level 1 is reserved for patients requiring immediate, life-saving intervention without delay, such as those in profound shock or unresponsive with severe respiratory distress.

allQuestions.text: During the primary trauma survey, which step involves controlling external hemorrhage and establishing large-bore IV access?
allQuestions.explanation: The "C" in the ABCs of trauma resuscitation stands for Circulation, which includes assessing pulses, controlling external bleeding, and obtaining IV access for fluids or blood. Airway and Breathing precede Circulation, while Disability refers to the neurological exam. Bleeding must be controlled before resuscitation can proceed effectively.

allQuestions.text: An unconscious trauma patient arrives in the ED with no family present. Under which legal doctrine can the emergency physician proceed with life-saving treatment without formal consent?
allQuestions.explanation: The Implied consent (Doctrine of Emergency) presumes that an unconscious patient with a life-threatening condition would consent to life-saving treatment, allowing physicians to act without formal consent. Informed consent requires an awake, capable patient to explicitly agree. Advance directives and guardianship require pre-existing documentation or a decision-maker, which are unavailable in this scenario.

allQuestions.text: A patient with massive, un-survivable trauma undergoes prolonged CPR despite no realistic chance of recovery. This scenario best illustrates which ethical concept?
allQuestions.explanation: Medical futility refers to interventions unlikely to produce meaningful benefit, such as prolonged CPR on a patient with un-survivable injuries. Physicians are not ethically obligated to provide futile care, though communicating this to families requires empathy. Beneficence and justice relate to providing benefit and fair resource allocation, not the specific concept of non-beneficial intervention.

allQuestions.text: Which zone of the emergency department is reserved for ESI Level 1 patients such as cardiac arrests and major traumas requiring full team mobilization?
allQuestions.explanation: The Trauma/Resus Bay consists of large, heavily equipped rooms reserved for the most critical ESI Level 1 patients requiring full team mobilization. Fast Track handles minor ESI 4/5 complaints, while the Main ED manages ESI 2–3 patients needing detailed workups. The waiting room and outpatient clinic are not part of acute in-department care.

allQuestions.text: A trauma patient presents with hypotension, tachycardia, and active external hemorrhage. Which type of shock is most consistent with this presentation?
allQuestions.explanation: Active external hemorrhage with hypotension and tachycardia is classic for hypovolemic shock, requiring immediate hemorrhage control and massive transfusion. Cardiogenic and obstructive shock arise from pump or mechanical obstruction problems, not blood loss, while distributive shock stems from vasodilation such as in sepsis. Rapidly diagnosing the shock type is essential to initiate the correct targeted therapy.

allQuestions.text: A patient in a hospital lacking a neurosurgeon requires specialized neurosurgical care not available at that facility. Which disposition option is most appropriate?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Transfer to a specialized facility
allQuestions.explanation: Transfer is indicated when a patient requires specialized care unavailable at the current facility, such as neurosurgery. Admission is appropriate only if the needed resources exist on-site, and discharge home is unsafe for a patient with an unresolved emergent condition. This disposition ensures the patient reaches definitive, appropriate care safely.

allQuestions.text: Hospital-wide bed shortages cause admitted patients to remain in the ED for extended periods. This phenomenon, known as "boarding," most directly compromises which of the four pillars of medical ethics due to the resulting overcrowding and delayed care for new arrivals?
allQuestions.explanation: Boarding creates severe overcrowding that compromises justice by disrupting fair and equitable allocation of ED resources among patients. This systemic issue also directly increases patient mortality.

allQuestions.text: A patient has a documented Do Not Intubate (DNI) order but develops worsening respiratory distress. Which of the following interventions would still be appropriate under this order?
options: Non-invasive support such as BiPAP or medications
originalOptions: Non-invasive support such as BiPAP or medications
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Non-invasive support such as BiPAP or medications
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Non-invasive support such as BiPAP or medications
allQuestions.explanation: A DNI order specifically prohibits placement of a breathing tube, but other treatments such as BiPAP or medications may still be given. Endotracheal intubation, RSI, surgical airway, and mechanical ventilation via ET tube all involve tube placement and are excluded by this order. Distinguishing DNI from DNR is essential, as DNI does not prohibit all supportive care.

allQuestions.text: A patient arrives at the ED with no pulse, no respiratory effort, and obvious signs of death (rigor mortis). To which triage area should this patient be assigned?
allQuestions.explanation: The Black area (or tag) is designated for patients who are deceased or have injuries incompatible with life. Unlike the Red area, which is for salvageable critically ill patients, resources are not directed toward resuscitation of patients already confirmed dead.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents to the ED with a minor laceration requiring simple wound closure, stable vital signs, and no other complaints. Which triage/care pathway is most appropriate?
allQuestions.explanation: Fast Track is designed for low-acuity patients (ESI 4–5) such as those with simple lacerations, minor illnesses, or issues requiring only one or zero resources. This pathway allows for rapid throughput without occupying acute care resources

allQuestions.text: Which of the following best describes the primary goal of resuscitation as one of the three pillars of emergency care?
options: Immediate stabilization of vital signs, taking the highest priority for the EM physician
Determining the safest next step for the patient
originalOptions: Immediate stabilization of vital signs, taking the highest priority for the EM physician
Determining the safest next step for the patient
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Immediate stabilization of vital signs, taking the highest priority for the EM physician
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Immediate stabilization of vital signs, taking the highest priority for the EM physician
allQuestions.explanation: Resuscitation is the first and highest priority among the three pillars of emergency care (Resuscitation, Diagnosis, Disposition). Stabilizing the patient's vital signs takes precedence over reaching a definitive diagnosis or determining disposition, since an unstable patient may die before either can occur.

allQuestions.text: A physician determines that continuing CPR on a patient with massive, un-survivable trauma would provide no meaningful benefit. What is this concept called, and what is the physician's ethical obligation?
options: Beneficence; the physician must continue regardless of family wishes
Justice; the physician must involve the ethics committee before any decision
Medical futility; the physician is not ethically obligated to provide futile care
Autonomy; the family has full authority to demand continued care
Non-maleficence; the physician must transfer the patient immediately
originalOptions: Beneficence; the physician must continue regardless of family wishes

Medical futility; the physician is not ethically obligated to provide futile care

allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Medical futility; the physician is not ethically obligated to provide futile care
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Medical futility; the physician is not ethically obligated to provide futile care
allQuestions.explanation: Medical futility refers to interventions unlikely to produce meaningful benefit. Physicians are not ethically obligated to provide futile care, though communicating this to a grieving family requires empathy and clear communication, and may involve the ethics committee when conflict arises.

allQuestions.text: A pulseless patient is found in the ED. Bystanders begin CPR immediately while another staff member activates the emergency response. To which triage area does this patient belong?
allQuestions.explanation: Any pulseless patient requires immediate resuscitation and is classified as Red area (ESI Level 1), reflecting the need for immediate, life-saving intervention. This differs from the Black area, which is reserved for patients already confirmed deceased or with injuries incompatible with life.

allQuestions.text: A patient with a new complaint visits her family physician first, who then decides whether specialist referral or hospital admission is needed. This reflects which core principle of Family Medicine?
allQuestions.explanation: First Contact Care means the family physician is typically the initial point of entry into the healthcare system, deciding whether further specialist or hospital care is needed. Continuity, comprehensiveness, and coordination describe ongoing or multi-domain aspects of care rather than this initial gatekeeping role.

allQuestions.text: A physician who has followed the same patient for eight years, reviewing his blood pressure, HbA1c, and personal circumstances at each visit, best demonstrates which principle?
allQuestions.explanation: Continuity of Care refers to a physician remaining consistently involved with a patient over time, building a longitudinal understanding of their condition and life circumstances. While comprehensive and patient-centered care are also relevant to good practice, the defining feature here is the long-term, ongoing relationship.

allQuestions.text: A physician evaluating a patient's knee pain who also reviews her hypertension, vaccination status, and screens for depression is demonstrating which principle?
allQuestions.explanation: Comprehensive Care means addressing all aspects of a patient's health during a single encounter, not just the presenting complaint. Coordination instead refers to organizing care between multiple providers, which is not the focus of this scenario.

allQuestions.text: A physician who reviews a hospital discharge summary, reconciles medications, and arranges follow-up with a cardiologist and endocrinologist is demonstrating which principle?
allQuestions.explanation: Coordination of Care involves organizing a patient's treatment and follow-up across multiple specialists and care settings, as shown by reconciling medications and arranging specialist follow-up. Comprehensive care instead refers to addressing multiple health domains within one visit, not coordinating between providers.

allQuestions.text: Which statement best reflects the concept of patient-centered care as emphasized by Sir William Osler?
options: The great physician treats the disease rather than the patient who has it
The good physician treats the disease, the great physician treats the patient who has the disease
The great physician treats only patients who actively request treatment
The good physician treats the patient's family rather than the patient
The great physician avoids exploring the patient's personal ideas and concerns
originalOptions: The great physician treats the disease rather than the patient who has it
The good physician treats the disease, the great physician treats the patient who has the disease
The great physician treats only patients who actively request treatment
The good physician treats the patient's family rather than the patient
The great physician avoids exploring the patient's personal ideas and concerns
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) The good physician treats the disease, the great physician treats the patient who has the disease
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The good physician treats the disease, the great physician treats the patient who has the disease
allQuestions.explanation: Osler's quote captures the essence of patient-centered care, distinguishing a good physician who focuses only on disease from a great physician who focuses on the whole patient. The other options invert or distort this principle.

allQuestions.text: A government imposes a tax on sugar-sweetened beverages to reduce future population-wide obesity risk before individuals develop unhealthy habits. This represents which level of prevention?
options: Primary prevention, since it targets an existing risk factor
Secondary prevention, since it detects disease early
Primordial prevention, since it prevents the emergence of risk factors themselves
Tertiary prevention, since it reduces complications of established disease
Quaternary prevention, since it avoids unnecessary medical intervention
originalOptions: Primary prevention, since it targets an existing risk factor
Secondary prevention, since it detects disease early
Primordial prevention, since it prevents the emergence of risk factors themselves
Tertiary prevention, since it reduces complications of established disease
Quaternary prevention, since it avoids unnecessary medical intervention
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Primordial prevention, since it prevents the emergence of risk factors themselves
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Primordial prevention, since it prevents the emergence of risk factors themselves
allQuestions.explanation: Primordial prevention aims to prevent risk factors from emerging in the first place by shaping healthy social and environmental conditions, such as taxing sugary drinks before unhealthy habits develop. This differs from primary prevention, which controls or eliminates risk factors that already exist.

allQuestions.text: A physician avoids ordering a routine chest x-ray for a patient with a self-limited viral upper respiratory infection, recognizing that further imaging would not change management. This reflects which level of prevention?
allQuestions.explanation: Quaternary prevention involves protecting patients from unnecessary or potentially harmful medical interventions, such as avoiding routine imaging that offers no clinical benefit. This is distinct from primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention, which involve actively intervening on risk factors, disease detection, or complications.

allQuestions.text: A 58-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes undergoes an annual retinal examination and foot examination to detect early complications, while his physician also counsels him on medication adherence. Which level of prevention does this scenario best represent?
options: Primary prevention only, since it addresses an existing risk factor
Secondary prevention only, since retinal screening detects asymptomatic disease
Tertiary prevention, since it aims to prevent complications in a patient with established disease
Primordial prevention, since it targets social conditions before disease onset
Quaternary prevention, since it avoids unnecessary intervention
originalOptions: Primary prevention only, since it addresses an existing risk factor
Secondary prevention only, since retinal screening detects asymptomatic disease
Tertiary prevention, since it aims to prevent complications in a patient with established disease
Primordial prevention, since it targets social conditions before disease onset
Quaternary prevention, since it avoids unnecessary intervention
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Tertiary prevention, since it aims to prevent complications in a patient with established disease
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Tertiary prevention, since it aims to prevent complications in a patient with established disease
allQuestions.explanation: Because the patient already has established diabetes, screening for complications such as retinopathy and counseling on adherence falls under tertiary prevention, which aims to reduce complications and disability in patients with existing disease. This is a common exam trap, since annual retinal screening superficially resembles secondary prevention, but the key distinction is that the underlying disease is already present.

allQuestions.text: According to the biopsychosocial model applied in Family Medicine, which combination of domains must a family physician integrate during every consultation?
options: Biological, environmental, and economic factors only
Sociological and biological factors only, excluding psychological factors
originalOptions: Biological, environmental, and economic factors only
Sociological and biological factors only, excluding psychological factors
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Biological, psychological, and sociological factors
allQuestions.explanation: The biopsychosocial model requires family physicians to integrate biological, psychological, and sociological dimensions of a patient's health during every consultation. The distractors substitute unrelated domains or omit one of the three core components.

allQuestions.text: A 62-year-old woman with symptomatic gallstones is informed of the risks and benefits of laparoscopic cholecystectomy by her surgeon. She states she understands the recommendation but declines surgery. The physician documents the discussion, ensures she understands the consequences, and respects her decision while discussing alternative management. Which two ethical principles are most directly demonstrated together in this scenario?
allQuestions.explanation: This scenario demonstrates autonomy through informed refusal, where the patient understands the consequences of declining treatment and the physician documents this understanding as part of informed consent. Justice, confidentiality, and beneficence are not the central principles being tested here, since the scenario centers on the patient's right to make an informed decision about her own care.

allQuestions.text: A 68-year-old man is newly diagnosed with colon cancer after biopsy. He asks his family physician direct questions about his prognosis. The physician answers honestly and compassionately rather than withholding or softening the diagnosis. Which ethical principle is being demonstrated?
allQuestions.explanation: Veracity refers to the physician's duty to tell the patient the truth about their diagnosis and prognosis, even when the news is difficult. Autonomy concerns respecting the patient's right to decide, and confidentiality concerns protecting information, neither of which is the focus here.

allQuestions.text: A 66-year-old man with established chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is enrolled in a pulmonary rehabilitation program and counseled on smoking cessation to slow disease progression and prevent further decline. Which level of prevention does this represent?
allQuestions.explanation: Because the patient already has established COPD, smoking cessation and rehabilitation here aim to reduce complications and disability rather than prevent disease onset, making this tertiary prevention. This differs from primary prevention, where smoking cessation would be used to prevent COPD from developing in the first place.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT one of the "4 Cs" core principles of Family Medicine?
allQuestions.explanation: The "4 Cs" are First Contact, Continuity, Comprehensive, and Coordination of Care, which distinguish Family Medicine from hospital-based specialties. Patient-centered care is an important additional principle in Family Medicine but is not one of the original 4 Cs.

allQuestions.text: A hospital has only one dialysis slot available for multiple patients in need. The care team prioritizes patients using transparent, objective medical criteria rather than social status, connections, or ability to pay. Which ethical principle is most directly demonstrated?
allQuestions.explanation: Justice requires fair and equitable distribution of limited healthcare resources based on objective medical criteria rather than social or financial factors. Beneficence and nonmaleficence relate to benefiting or not harming an individual patient, not to fair allocation across multiple patients.

allQuestions.text: A patient living in a remote village is able to reach basic family medicine services without excessive travel or cost, as the clinic was deliberately placed within reasonable geographic reach of the local population. Which essential attribute of primary care does this best illustrate?
allQuestions.explanation: Accessibility refers to primary care being geographically reachable so that patients, including those in remote areas, can obtain care without excessive burden. Comprehensiveness instead refers to the breadth of services offered, not geographic reach.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following best describes the scope of urology as a specialty?
options: Surgical specialty dealing with diseases of the urinary tract and male genital tract
Medical specialty limited to glomerulonephritis and interstitial nephritis
Specialty limited to female reproductive disorders
Specialty exclusively managing chronic kidney impairment
Specialty limited to prostate cancer screening
originalOptions: Surgical specialty dealing with diseases of the urinary tract and male genital tract
Medical specialty limited to glomerulonephritis and interstitial nephritis
Specialty limited to female reproductive disorders
Specialty exclusively managing chronic kidney impairment
Specialty limited to prostate cancer screening
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Surgical specialty dealing with diseases of the urinary tract and male genital tract
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Surgical specialty dealing with diseases of the urinary tract and male genital tract
allQuestions.explanation: Urology is defined as the surgical specialty managing diseases of the urinary tract and male genital tract, using both medical and surgical management. Nephrology, in contrast, medically manages conditions such as chronic kidney impairment, glomerulonephritis, and interstitial nephritis.

allQuestions.text: Regarding the vertical position of the kidneys relative to the vertebral column, which statement is correct?
options: The left kidney is 1–2 cm below the right kidney
The right kidney extends from the 1st to the 3rd lumbar vertebrae, and is 1–2 cm lower than the left
Both kidneys are at the same vertebral level
The right kidney extends from the 12th thoracic to the 3rd lumbar vertebrae, and is 1–2 cm lower than the left
The left kidney is located entirely within the pelvis
